title: What Should Enterprise AI Prove Before the Next Investment?
subtitle: A practical guide to deciding when an AI pilot deserves more funding, wider use, stronger controls or a different direction.
excerpt: An AI pilot can demonstrate technical promise without proving that the organization should expand it. Before approving more funding, leadership needs evidence of changed business work, reliable performance, clear responsibility for data and actions, and the full cost of operating the service. These tests help executives choose whether to expand, redesign, continue learning or stop.
content_html:
Consider an enterprise AI pilot that helps a commercial operations team prepare its weekly performance reviews. The assistant retrieves approved reports, identifies unusual movements in sales data and drafts explanations for managers to examine. The demonstrations are promising, employees find the tool useful, and the business sponsor wants to make it available across more regions.

The next proposal asks for additional funding, deeper connections to business systems and greater freedom for the AI to perform tasks automatically. The technical team can explain how these capabilities would work. The investment committee now has to decide whether they would improve the business outcome enough to justify their cost and added responsibility.

This is where enterprise AI investment decisions deserve more attention. A successful pilot establishes that a capability can work under certain conditions. Expanding it requires evidence that the organization can depend on the service, support it and benefit from it in everyday operations.

My work leading AI portfolio assessment and governance design has reinforced a practical principle: fund the next level of AI capability against the business problem it will solve, the responsibility it introduces and the evidence that supports the investment.

What has the first investment actually achieved?

The commercial operations pilot may have produced accurate summaries and reduced the effort of preparing initial reports. Those are useful results if they have been measured. They are also only part of the work that managers ultimately need to complete.

A weekly performance review includes interpreting figures, resolving conflicting explanations, agreeing corrective actions and following through on decisions. If AI prepares the analysis faster but managers still spend the same time validating information or waiting for other departments, the improvement may be smaller than the demonstration suggests.

Before approving expansion, I want to understand which parts of that work have changed. Did the team complete reviews more quickly? Were explanations accurate enough to use? Did employees spend less time correcting outputs? Were business decisions made sooner, or did the improvement remain limited to preparing the material?

The distinction helps determine what to fund next. If retrieval quality is the principal constraint, better information management may deserve investment. If reviews are delayed by unclear responsibilities, changing the approval process may be more useful than introducing another AI agent. If the existing assistant already completes its assigned task reliably, the organization may have little reason to make it more complex.

Data, knowledge, models, agents, connections, permissions and operations all play a part in enterprise AI. Each adds capability and responsibility. The business task should determine which components are needed and when their additional complexity deserves further investment.

Different leaders can reasonably reach different conclusions

An expansion proposal rarely belongs to one department. Several stakeholders may agree that the AI pilot is promising while holding different views about what should happen next.

The business sponsor may prioritize faster decisions and wider access. Finance will want to understand the full cost of serving additional teams. IT may support the expansion while raising concerns about system dependencies, permissions and ongoing maintenance. Employees may question whether the underlying data is sufficiently reliable, particularly when AI-generated explanations conflict with their knowledge of customers or local operating conditions.

These are legitimate business concerns. Effective leadership means bringing them into the same investment discussion and determining which questions must be resolved before the organization commits further resources.

Take a seemingly straightforward request to let the AI update customer records. The application may already have the technical capability to make those changes. That does not establish whether the system has permission to do so, which fields it can modify, who is accountable for an incorrect update or how the organization would recover from a mistake.

The decision depends on the consequences of the action. A low-risk draft can reasonably be handled differently from an automated change that affects customers, contracts or financial records. I would keep human approval where the consequences justify it and expand automated authority only when the controls and operating evidence support that choice. That also raises the question of how an employee is prepared and authorized to challenge AI recommendations, which I examine in Who Is Testing the Person Asked to Challenge AI?

Knowledge introduces a similar responsibility. If two regions use different definitions of an active customer, an AI assistant may reproduce those differences in its analysis. Before blaming the model, the organization needs to establish which definition applies and who has authority to resolve the conflict. I explored this problem in AI Can Find Your Company's Knowledge. But Who Decides What It Can Trust?

These questions should influence funding decisions because they determine whether expansion is genuinely ready. Better technology can help resolve some difficulties, but investment cannot substitute for business ownership or decisions that the organization has yet to make.

The next budget must include the service people will actually operate

Model prices and infrastructure costs are relatively visible. The work required to keep an AI service dependable can be harder to estimate, especially when a pilot has relied on a small team providing informal support.

As the service expands, someone must maintain data sources, review permissions, investigate incorrect results, test application changes and support employees when something goes wrong. The organization also needs a workable way to monitor service quality and respond when an AI-generated recommendation creates an exception.

For that reason, I prefer to evaluate the total cost of a correctly completed business task rather than the cost of an individual model response. The comparison should include employee review, corrections, support and any additional work transferred to another team. A less expensive model is not necessarily the cheaper business option if it generates substantial rework. A more capable model is not necessarily justified when existing tools already perform the task adequately.

Reliability belongs in that calculation. An assistant may perform well under normal conditions but become unavailable when a connected system fails. If employees cannot access critical information or complete their work through an approved alternative, the operational consequence extends beyond the AI application itself.

I explored the broader responsibility for technology dependencies in From US Tech Outages to a Bigger Question: Who Controls AI's Consequences? The practical lesson for AI investment is that recovery, support and service ownership need to be designed and funded alongside new capabilities.

The appropriate level of control will vary. A read-only assistant used for internal analysis does not require the same safeguards as an agent authorized to alter business records. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework and OWASP guidance on excessive agency offer useful references for evaluating these responsibilities. The organization still needs to decide which risks are acceptable for its particular work.

Make the next investment decision explicit

An AI investment review should finish with a clear decision about what the organization is prepared to fund and operate.

For the commercial operations example, I would bring together four pieces of evidence: the business outcome compared with the original baseline; the quality and reliability of the service; the responsibilities, permissions and support required for expansion; and the complete cost of the next stage.

The organization may continue a limited trial while correcting data-quality problems. It may change the design if a simpler approach could deliver the same benefit. It may approve expansion to another region when the evidence and local operating conditions support it. Or it may stop an initiative whose additional cost and risk no longer justify the expected result.

Any expansion also needs a named business owner responsible for the outcome, alongside clear responsibility for information quality, technical operations and exception handling. These responsibilities cannot disappear when the pilot team moves on to another initiative.

There is a reasonable argument for keeping early AI experimentation lightweight. I support that. Requiring the full controls of a production service before an organization has tested a simple idea can consume resources without improving learning. A contained experiment needs proportionate safeguards and clear permission to operate within its boundaries.

The decision changes when the service begins affecting more people, more systems or more consequential actions. At that point, the organization needs stronger evidence because the responsibilities have expanded as well.

I would support a more capable AI design when it demonstrably removes a business constraint that the simpler service cannot address. That could mean reducing manual effort in a controlled workflow, improving decision quality or performing narrowly defined actions more reliably. The proposed improvement must be weighed against the additional cost, operating responsibilities and possible consequences of failure.

The most useful result of the next investment meeting is a decision that connects what the business has learned, what it is authorizing and what it expects to improve. Before funding the next model, agent or connection to another system, ask the team to demonstrate which part of the work will become better and who will take responsibility for keeping that improvement in place. That gives the business a sound basis to invest, change direction or stop.
